questions.question: Arrange the following events in correct chronology: 1) Champaran Satyagraha against indigo plantation 2) Starting of non-cooperation Khilafat movement 3) Rowlatt Satyagraha 4) Arrival of Simon commission in India
questions.questionHtml:
Arrange the following events in correct chronology:

1) Champaran Satyagraha against indigo plantation
2) Starting of non-cooperation Khilafat movement
3) Rowlatt Satyagraha
4) Arrival of Simon commission in India
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1-3-2-4.

Important Points

  • Champaran Satyagraha against indigo plantation was in 1917.
    • Champaran Satyagraha was Mahathma Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.
    • It took place at Champaran in Bihar.
    • Demand for high rent and illegal dues by European planters leads to Champaran Satyagraha.
    • British agreed to the demands of the farmers at the end of this satyagraha.
  • Rowlatt Satyagraha was in 1919.
    • It was against the anarchical and revolutionary crimes act(Rowlett act) passed by the British.
    • The Rowlett act was passed on 6th February 1919.
    • Gandhiji called this act as "black act'".
    • The act empowered the British government to arrest any person without reason, search any place without warrant and imprison anyone without trial.
  • The Non-cooperation Khilafat movement was started in 1920.
    • The non-cooperation movement is the first mass political movement under Gandhiji in India.
    • The attainment of swaraj by peaceful means was the main goal of this movement.
    • The non-cooperation movement was called off by Gandhiji due to the Chauri Chaura incident.
  • The Simon commission arrived in India in 1928.
    • It was formed to study constitutional reforms and make recommendations to the government in India.
    • Simon commission was an all-white commission without any Indian members.
    • It was formed on 26th November 1927.
    • Simon commission arrived in India on 3rd February 1928.
    • Simon commission submitted its reports on 27th May 1930.

questions.question: Who is regarded as the ‘Mother of Indian Revolution’?
questions.questionHtml: Who is regarded as the ‘Mother of Indian Revolution’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Madame Cama

Key Points

  • Madame Cama is widely regarded as the 'Mother of Indian Revolution'.
  • She was an important figure in the Indian independence movement and played a crucial role in advocating for India's freedom from British rule.
  • Madame Cama was known for her fiery speeches and was deeply involved in the revolutionary activities against the British Empire.
  • She also unfurled the first version of the Indian national flag in 1907 at the International Socialist Conference in Stuttgart, Germany.
  • Her contributions to the freedom struggle were significant, and she inspired many young revolutionaries to join the cause.

Additional Information

  • Madame Bhikaji Cama was born on 24th September 1861 in Bombay (now Mumbai).
  • She was a strong advocate for gender equality and worked tirelessly for the upliftment of women in society.
  • Madame Cama was influenced by the social and political conditions of her time and was determined to fight against the injustices perpetrated by the British colonial rulers.
  • She spent a significant part of her life in exile in Europe, where she continued her revolutionary activities and garnered international support for India's independence.
  • Madame Cama passed away on 13th August 1936, but her legacy continues to inspire generations of Indians.

questions.question: What was the Swadeshi Movement called in the state of Andhra Pradesh?
questions.questionHtml: What was the Swadeshi Movement called in the state of Andhra Pradesh?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Vande Mataram Movement

Key Points

  • The Swadeshi Movement in Andhra Pradesh was known as the Vande Mataram Movement.
  • This movement was part of the larger Indian independence movement aimed at boycotting British goods and promoting Indian goods.
  • The term "Vande Mataram" translates to "I bow to thee, Mother" and was a slogan used to evoke nationalistic sentiments.
  • It played a significant role in uniting people from different regions of India in the fight against British rule.

Additional Information

  • The Swadeshi Movement was officially started in 1905 as a response to the partition of Bengal by the British government.
  • It involved various forms of protests such as boycotts, strikes, and the promotion of indigenous industries.
  • Leaders like Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai were prominent figures in the Swadeshi Movement.
  • The movement laid the foundation for future nationalistic movements and played a crucial role in India's struggle for independence.

questions.question: Rulers of mahajanapadas in ancient India collected a tax called ‘Bhaga’ from the _____ in their region.
questions.questionHtml: Rulers of mahajanapadas in ancient India collected a tax called ‘Bhaga’ from the _____ in their region.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Farmers.

Key Points

  • Rulers of mahajanapadas in ancient India collected a tax called ‘Bhaga’ from the Farmers in their region.
  • Mahajanapadas:
    • As the rulers of the Mahajanapadas were building huge forts, maintaining big armies, they needed more resources.
    • And they needed officials to collect these. So, instead of depending on occasional gifts brought by people, as in the case of the Raja of the Janapadas, they started collecting regular taxes.
    • Taxes on crops were the most important.
    • This was because agriculture was the main occupation at that time. Usually, the tax was fixed at 1/6th of what was produced.
    • This was known as bhaga or a share.
    • There were taxes on craftspersons as well. These could have been in the form of labour.
    • For example, a weaver or a smith may have had to work for a day every month for the king.
    • Herders were also expected to pay taxes in the form of animals and animal products.
    • There were also taxes on goods that were bought and sold, through trade. And hunters and gatherers also had to provide forest produce to the raja.

questions.question: After the revolt of 1857, which of the following changes were NOT introduced by the British Government in India?
questions.questionHtml: After the revolt of 1857, which of the following changes were NOT introduced by the British Government in India?

options.text: Governor General of India became Viceroy of India
options.html: Governor General of India became Viceroy of India

options.text: Secretary of State for India was appointed
options.html: Secretary of State for India was appointed

options.text: Powers of East India Company was transferred to British Crown
options.html: Powers of East India Company was transferred to British Crown

options.text: Proportion of India Soldiers in the British army were increased
options.html: Proportion of India Soldiers in the British army were increased

questions.solution:
• The revolt of 1857 was a big jolt to the authority of East India Company in India and also a shock to the Crown in England. Hence, Her Majesty's government in England enacted the Government of India Act, 1858 to improve administration in India and thus this act came to be known as the act of good government in India. This act made certain changes like:
    • The administration of territories in India was taken over the Cabinet in Britain from the Company. This was announced in Darbar at Allahabad on 1st November 1858 and is known as Queen's Proclamation.
    • To reduce the future possibilities of revolt in the military, the number of Europeans was increased and that of Indians were decreased.
    • The post of the governor-general of India was made as to the viceroy of India and he was to be the representative of Queen in India. Lord Canning became the first viceroy of India.
    • Viceroy was provided with an executive council of 4 members to assist him in the discharge of his duties.
    • A secretary of state was appointed in London from the existing cabinet who was the in-charge of Indian affairs.

questions.question: Who among the following was NOT a minister of Cabinet Mission Plan, 1946?

  • The three-member mission visited India between March and June 1946. The delegation of British ministers included Lord Pethick-Lawrence, Sir Stafford Cripps and Mr. A.V. Alexander.

Key Proposals of the Cabinet Mission Plan:

  1. Rejected the demand for a sovereign Pakistan.
  2. Grouping of existing assemblies into 3 sections A, B, C.
  3. Provincial autonomy and residual powers.

questions.question: The Ryotwari (Peasant) System of 1820 was implemented in which of the following regions?
questions.questionHtml: The Ryotwari (Peasant) System of 1820 was implemented in which of the following regions?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Madras and BombayKey Points

  • The Ryotwari System was introduced by the British under Thomas Munro and Sir John Malcolm in the early 19th century (around 1820) as a way to collect land revenue directly from the peasants (known as "ryots").
  • Madras (now Tamil Nadu) and Bombay (now Mumbai, including parts of Gujarat) were the main regions where this system was implemented.
  • In the Ryotwari system, the government dealt directly with individual farmers, rather than through intermediaries like zamindars (landlords), as was the case in the Zamindari System.
  • Under the Ryotwari system, the peasants were required to pay a fixed land revenue, and the amount was assessed based on the quality of the land.
  • It was implemented in parts of southern and western India, particularly in Madras (Tamil Nadu) and Bombay (Maharashtra).

questions.question: In 1824 the sepoys refused to go to which place to fight for the East India Company by sea route?
questions.questionHtml: In 1824 the sepoys refused to go to which place to fight for the East India Company by sea route?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Burma

Explanation:

In 1824 the Sepoys were asked to go to Burma by the sea route to fight for the Company. In 1824, during the First Anglo-Burmese War (1824–1826), the sepoys (Indian soldiers serving in the British East India Company's army) refused to board ships to go to Burma. The conflict arose primarily due to the sepoys' objections to crossing the "Kalapani" or "Black Water," which was a term used to refer to the sea.

The sepoys, who were accustomed to land-based warfare, were hesitant and superstitious about crossing the sea. The concept of overseas travel and fighting across the seas went against their traditional beliefs and practices. The refusal to board ships created a significant challenge for the British East India Company, as they had to find alternative means to transport their forces to Burma.

The reluctance of the sepoys to go by sea was a notable incident during the First Anglo-Burmese War and highlighted the cultural and religious factors influencing the behavior of Indian soldiers serving under the British East India Company. The British East India Company had to address such concerns and adapt their strategies to accommodate the preferences and beliefs of the sepoys in order to maintain their military effectiveness in overseas campaigns.

questions.question: Which of the following was the first fort by English East India Company in India?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following was the first fort by English East India Company in India?
questions.solution:
Option 2 is correct, i.e. Fort St.George.

Important Points

Fort built by the English East India Company in India are:

  • Fort St. George is the first English (later British) fortress in India, founded in 1639 at the coastal city of Madras, the modern city of Chennai.
    • The construction of the fort provided the impetus for further settlements and trading activity, in what was originally an uninhabited land.
    • Thus, it is a feasible contention to say that the city evolved around the fortress.
  • Sewri Fort was built by Britishers in 1680 in Mumbai.
  • Fort William was built in 1696 by the East India Company by John Goldsborough at Calcutta.
  • Masulipatnam fort was built in the 17th century as an attachment to a textile factory by officials. After the cyclone of 1864, it was transformed into a memorial to those who lost their lives in the disaster.

Thus, we can conclude that Fort St.George is the first English fortress in India.

Additional Information

English East India Company:

  • The East India Company first arrived via sea route at Surat in the year 1608 for the purpose of establishing trade with India.
  • The Battle of Plassey was a decisive victory of the British East India Company over the Nawab of Bengal Siraj-Ud-Daulah and his French allies on 23 June 1757.

questions.question: In 1943, some of the younger leaders in which district of Maharashtra set up a parallel government (Prati Sarkar), with volunteer corps (Seba dals) and village units (Tufan dals )?
questions.questionHtml: In 1943, some of the younger leaders in which district of Maharashtra set up a parallel government (Prati Sarkar), with volunteer corps (Seba dals) and village units (Tufan dals )?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Satara.

Key Points

  • The Satara Parallel Government in Maharashtra, which fought British control from August 1943 to May 1946, was a legendary chapter in India's historic freedom war.
  • It, like the parallel administrations in Bengal's Midnapore, Bihar's Bhagalpur, Uttar Pradesh's Ballia, and Odisha's Basudevpur, was an armed outgrowth of the 1942 Quit India movement.
  • 'Kratisimha' Nana Patil (1900-1976), the leader of the Satara Parallel administration, later joined the Communist Party and was elected to the Lok Sabha on the CPI platform from Satara in 1957 and Beed in 1967.
  • The Prati Sarkar (Parallel Government) movement was a guerilla movement that operated in over 150 villages with widespread peasant backing.

Additional Information

  • Satara is a city in Maharashtra, located near the confluence of the Krishna River and its tributary, the Venna.
  • The city was founded in the 16th century and served as the capital of the Maratha Empire's Chhatrapati, Shahu I.

questions.question: Around 1810 AD, about ______% of indigo imported to Britain was from India.
questions.questionHtml: Around 1810 AD, about ______% of indigo imported to Britain was from India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 95.

Key Points

  • Around 1810 AD, about  95 % of indigo imported to Britain was from India.
  • Indigo cultivation :
    • It was often referred to as blue gold because of its high value as a trading commodity. It gives a blue hue to the fabrics.
    • The demand for Indigo increased considerably during the industrialization in Britain and so did its production.
    • The soil of India was highly suitable for the cultivation of Indigo and the Britishers forced Indian farmers to grow Indigo.
    • The Charter Act of 1833 gave rights to planters to exploit farmers. The loan offered to farmers was so high that farmers always remained in debt and they had to grow whatever their British Planters asked them to.
    • Almost all the fertile land went into growing indigo and farmers felt exploited in the hands of British planters.
    • By the late 19th century nearly all indigo came from indigo bush plantations in India.
    • Karl Heumann in Zurich in 1890 found a way of making better indigo colour from aniline.
    • BASF (now, a multinational chemical company) started the production of synthetic indigo in 1897. Soon, many companies came up with their improved versions of chemical colours and this led to the fall of Indigo cultivation in India.
    • Many farmers in India were left with tons of Indigo along with the debt and no one was willing to buy it.
    • Hence, we can say that Indigo cultivation in India declined by the beginning of the 20th century because of its unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions.
